ingredients.name: Lotus root (nelum ala)
ingredients.notes: peeled and sliced into 5mm rounds; submerge immediately in water with a little lime juice to prevent browning. Check inside each segment for mud before cooking -- the hollow channels can trap sediment.

ingredients.name: Curry leaves
ingredients.notes: 1 sprig, split between the main cook and the final temper

ingredients.name: Goraka
ingredients.notes: small piece; optional, adds characteristic sourness

ingredients.name: Thin coconut milk
ingredients.notes: or water; for the main cook

steps.instruction: Peel the lotus root and slice into 5mm rounds. Check each slice for mud inside the hollow channels and rinse thoroughly. Submerge the slices immediately in water with a squeeze of lime juice to prevent browning.

Place the drained lotus root in a saucepan. Add the onion, tomato, green chilli, half the curry leaves, pandan leaf, fenugreek, turmeric, chilli powder, curry powder, goraka (if using), Maldive fish flakes (if using), and salt.

Pour in the thin coconut milk (or water) to just cover the lotus root. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer covered for 15-18 minutes until the lotus root is just tender -- it should retain a slight crunch, similar to water chestnut. It should not disintegrate.
Add the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer uncovered over low heat for 3-5 minutes until the gravy thickens slightly.

Meanwhile, prepare the temper: heat the oil or ghee in a small pan. Fry the shallots until golden, then add the remaining curry leaves and Maldive fish (if using), and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour the temper over the finished curry. Taste and adjust salt. Sprinkle a little roasted curry powder on top if desired. Serve hot with rice.

source_site: hungrylankan.com, cross-checked against 196flavors.com, foodcnr.com, pulse.lk, akkiskitchen.com, infolanka.com, recipeland.com, bigoven.com, and cookingindex.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 9+ independent sources; consistent agreement on the basic coconut-milk curry technique; minor variation in whether to use goraka, the presence of a final temper, and whether to use fresh coconut paste as a thickener
notes: Lotus root (nelum ala) is an aquatic vegetable with a distinctive appearance -- when sliced crossways, the hollow channels form a beautiful flower-like pattern that makes it visually striking in a curry. The key texture point is preserving a slight crunch -- lotus root should never be cooked until mushy; it should retain the firm, slightly crunchy texture similar to water chestnut. The hollow channels can trap mud, particularly if the root is broken, so checking and rinsing each slice carefully is important. A fancier 'kalu pol' (black coconut) version exists using dry-roasted toasted coconut as a thickener (like the wattakka kalu pol technique), giving a darker, nuttier gravy -- this entry reflects the simpler, more commonly home-cooked coconut-milk version. A popular alternative treatment is lotus root chips -- peeled, sliced very thin, deep-fried, and lightly salted.
